findings.issue_text: [BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run completes the work item's offset in the finally block even when result_processor raises, so failed messages become committable and are committed by the commit loop, directly contradicting SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. A transient error (DB write failure, exception in handle_result) causes the uptime result to be silently dropped forever: the offset is marked complete, the 1s commit loop commits past it, and the message is never retried. The new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling encodes the opposite expectation (asserts committed_offsets stays empty) and only passes when it asserts before the 1-second commit loop fires — it is a flaky failure in CI whenever the commit lands first.

[BUG] create_thread_queue_parallel_worker reuses the factory's single FixedQueuePool on every create_with_partitions call, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (invoked by arroyo when a strategy is replaced) calls queue_pool.shutdown(), permanently killing all worker threads — so after any partition rebalance the factory hands the new strategy a dead pool. On a rebalance (consumer count changes, broker rebalance, partition revocation/reassignment — routine for the uptime-results consumer group), the recreated strategy submits messages into queues whose workers have exited and whose queue.Queue objects are shut down; items are never processed, offsets are never committed, consumer lag grows without bound, and the stall is silent. No test in the diff exercises a second create_with_partitions call on the same factory, so this path is entirely unverified.

[ADVISORY] Every queue is created as an unbounded queue.Queue() while the class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' — no maxsize is set anywhere in the pool. If workers fall behind (slow DB writes for one hot subscription hash bucket, or a dead pool per the rebalance bug), queue depth grows without limit and the process OOMs; the documented backpressure property does not exist, so operators sizing max_workers get no memory safety at all.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.shutdown relies on queue.Queue.shutdown(), which only exists in Python 3.13+; on earlier runtimes the AttributeError is swallowed by the except Exception, leaving every worker blocked forever in work_queue.get(). On a Python < 3.13 runtime, every shutdown (factory.shutdown, strategy.close, test tearDown) leaks 20+ daemon threads blocked on get(), and worker.join(timeout=5.0) burns 5 seconds per queue (100s for the default 20 queues) before returning — shutdowns hang and CI/test teardown time balloons. Verify the repo's minimum Python version before merging; if it is < 3.13 this is a P1 crash-on-shutdown, otherwise it is a portability landmine.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty is defined but never called anywhere in the diff, and WorkItem.message is populated on every item but never read by any code path. wait_until_empty is dead code that tests deliberately avoid in favor of hand-rolled polling loops (every new test reimplements the same stats/sleep wait), and WorkItem.message retains a full Message/BrokerValue reference per in-flight item for no consumer, adding per-item memory cost with no behavior — both are deletion candidates that force future readers to reason about unused surface.

[ADVISORY] The worker emits a metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth') call on every single processed item in the finally block, in addition to the poll()-level total_queued gauge. At uptime-results throughput this is one gauge flush per message consumed — metric volume (and qsize() lock contention) scales linearly with check results rather than with poll intervals, adding measurable agent overhead on the hot path for data the poll()-based gauge already reports.

[BUG] The worker's finally-block calls offset_tracker.complete_offset() even when result_processor raised, so failed messages' offsets are marked complete and subsequently committed, directly contradicting the strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing'. Any transient error in result_processor (e.g. a DB blip while recording an uptime check result) results in the message being silently dropped: the exception is logged, the offset is completed in finally, the commit loop advances past it, and the check result is never reprocessed — missed downtime incidents with no DLQ or retry path.

[BUG] ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() sets self.queue_pool = None, but arroyo re-invokes create_with_partitions() on the same factory instance after a rebalance, and create_thread_queue_parallel_worker() (line ~247) starts with 'assert self.queue_pool is not None', which now fails. On any consumer-group rebalance (or a second create_with_partitions call), the uptime results consumer crashes with AssertionError instead of building a new strategy; even without the assert, the surviving SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy would submit into already-shut-down queues whose worker threads are dead.

[BUG] The strategy's docstring promises 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but every queue is constructed as queue.Queue() with default maxsize=0 (unbounded) and submit() never blocks or checks depth, so the claimed backpressure invariant is not enforced anywhere. During consumer lag or a slow result_processor (e.g. DB contention), the StreamProcessor keeps polling and submit() keeps enqueueing without bound; the process's memory grows with the lag instead of throttling, ending in OOM kills rather than graceful slowdown.

[ADVISORY] _commit_loop reimplements offset-commit scheduling inside the strategy with a hardcoded 1.0s interval, bypassing the StreamProcessor's configured commit_policy (the new integration test even configures ONCE_PER_SECOND, which this loop ignores), creating a second, untraceable commit path alongside arroyo's. Operators tuning commit frequency via the standard arroyo commit policy get no effect in this mode; two independent commit mechanisms now exist in the codebase with different semantics (+1 handling lives in result_consumer.commit_offsets while interval lives here), so the next commit-related change must be made in two places and can silently diverge.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() has no caller anywhere in the diff — neither production code nor tests use it — making it speculative generality shipped inert. Dead code that the next maintainer must reason about (it polls qsize in a busy loop and has a timeout-vs-in-flight-work race: items still being processed count as 'empty' the moment they leave the queue), and it will drift from get_stats()/shutdown() semantics as the pool evolves.

[ADVISORY] WorkItem.message holds a full Message[KafkaPayload] per work item but is never read anywhere in the diff — neither by the worker, the strategy, nor any commit path. Every queued result retains its entire Kafka payload (key, value, headers) for the lifetime of the queue entry purely as dead weight, inflating memory under lag for no function; the field invites future misuse where code assumes it is still valid after processing.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool (and its num_queues worker threads) is constructed eagerly in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ rather than in create_with_partitions, so threads spawn at factory construction time before any consumer assignment exists. Every factory instantiation — including test setups, management commands, or tooling that merely builds the factory — spawns max_workers-or-20 daemon threads; combined with the shutdown()/None lifecycle this couples thread lifetime to the wrong object and is the root of the rebalance-crash path.

[BUG] OrderedQueueWorker.run catches Exception from result_processor, logs it, and then in the finally block calls offset_tracker.complete_offset, so a message whose processing failed is treated as successfully processed and its offset becomes committable. The strategy's documented guarantee 'Only commits offsets after successful processing' is violated: a failed uptime result is committed to Kafka as consumed and never redelivered, silently dropping check results (missed downtime/incident detection) — the old arroyo modes crash the processor on unhandled exceptions so messages are retried; this mode converts processing failures into permanent at-most-once delivery.

[BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's except block calls add_offset followed by complete_offset for the failing message, marking a message that was never processed as done. Any decode or grouping failure (e.g., a malformed payload) permanently drops that message while the offset is committed as processed — same silent data-loss failure mode as the worker path, at the submit site.

[BUG] OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets breaks at the first offset in [start, max_offset] that was never added via add_offset, and nothing ever fills that gap, so commits stall permanently at any missing offset. Real Kafka topics produce offset gaps (aborted transactions, log compaction); the new test_offset_gaps tests bake gap-blocking in as expected behavior, but unlike arroyo's built-in modes (which commit past gaps), this consumer's commits stop forever at the gap, causing unbounded consumer lag and unbounded growth of all_offsets until manual intervention — the tests' assumption that submitted offsets are gap-free-by-design does not hold for the production topic.

[BUG] FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize while SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' — no backpressure exists. When workers fall behind (e.g., a slow downstream in result_processor or a single hot subscription hashing to one queue), the affected queue grows without bound, consuming unbounded memory in the consumer process and eventually OOM-killing it, with no lag-based protection the docstring promises.

[BUG] submit passes message.payload directly to the decoder, but the production decoder (ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload) asserts not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload), so every FilteredPayload message raises AssertionError and is routed into the exception path. Every filtered message in production is logged as 'Error submitting message to queue' with a full stack trace (error-log spam proportional to filtered volume) and handled as a failure instead of the no-op the strategy's unit-test decoder implements; the unit test test_handles_invalid_messages only passes because it substitutes a custom decoder that does not have this assertion.

[ADVISORY] self.result_processor = self.result_processor_cls() was moved from the end of __init__ to the top, before max_batch_size/max_batch_time/input_block_size/output_block_size are assigned, to satisfy the new queue_pool branch. Any result_processor_cls whose constructor reads those attributes now observes pre-assignment values (None/defaults) in every mode, not just thread-queue-parallel — a silent initialization-order change to all existing serial/parallel/batched-parallel consumers introduced as a side effect of the new mode, who get bitten when a subclass constructor depends on that config.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool shutdown ownership is split between ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown (which also nulls the reference) and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/join, both of which shut down the same shared pool instance. In the normal arroyo lifecycle close() then join() (which calls close() again) shut the pool down twice per run, and factory.shutdown() plus strategy.close() in the tests exercise a third path; worse, if arroyo invokes create_with_partitions again after a close (restart within the process), the new strategy receives the already-shut-down pool whose workers have exited, so messages queue but are never processed and offsets never commit.

[ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that no commit occurs after a processing failure, which is the opposite of the implementation's behavior (the failed offset is completed and becomes committable). The test encodes drifted intent ('errors block commits') that the code does not implement; it only passes when the loop breaks before the commit thread's next 1-second tick, making it timing-flaky, and it documents a guarantee ('Only commits offsets after successful processing') that the shipped code violates — whoever trusts the test or the docstring will be wrong.

[ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty is never called anywhere in the diff (production code or tests). Dead code that implies a drain-before-shutdown behavior that shutdown() does not actually provide (shutdown discards queued items without waiting); deleting the method removes a misleading surface — the next reader may assume graceful drain exists when it does not.

[ADVISORY] WorkItem.message is populated on every submit but never read by any code in the diff. Every queued item retains the full Kafka Message (payload bytes included) in memory for the entire queue dwell time; deleting the field shrinks per-item memory and removes dead state — this compounds the unbounded-queue memory growth since payloads are held twice (payload and result).

[ADVISORY] The generic OrderedQueueWorker hardcodes a 'monitors.' prefix into the sentry_sdk transaction name (f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}") for a component used by non-monitors consumers such as the uptime results consumer. Uptime (and any future ResultsStrategyFactory consumer) trace transactions are mislabeled under the monitors namespace, so engineers filtering dashboards/alerts by transaction name for the uptime consumer will not find or will misattribute its worker spans.

[ADVISORY] OrderedQueueWorker.run emits the remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth gauge inside the finally block, i.e., once per processed item per worker thread. Metric emission volume scales linearly with message throughput across all queue workers instead of being sampled or emitted from poll(), adding measurable metrics cost and cardinality on the hottest path in the consumer.

adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` even when `result_processor` raises (caught by the broad `except Exception`). The added uptime test `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling` is consistent with being flaky: it asserts no commit happened, but the commit thread runs every 1s and can commit failed offsets once the worker marks them complete.

adjudication.rationale: In `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, `self.queue_pool` is created once for `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` and then reused in every `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` call (`queue_pool=self.queue_pool`). adjudication.rationale: In `OrderedQueueWorker.run`, any exception from `self.result_processor(...)` is caught by the broad `except Exception:` and only logged, and then the `finally` block unconditionally calls `self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset)` (new file `queue_consumer.py`). `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop` then uses `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets()` to commit offsets without any success/failure signal. This means failed processing is still marked complete and can become committable/committed, contradicting the strategy docstring guarantee "Only commits offsets after successful processing" and risking silent loss (no redelivery) on processing errors.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit's except block calls add_offset followed by complete_offset for the failing message, marking a message that was never processed as done. Any decode or grouping failure (e.g., a malformed payload) permanently drops that message while the offset is committed as processed — same silent data-loss failure mode as the worker path, at the submit site.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, any exception in decoding/grouping/work item creation is caught and then, if `message.value` is a `BrokerValue`, the code explicitly calls `add_offset(...)` followed by `complete_offset(...)` for that same offset. This makes the offset immediately committable by the commit loop even though the message was not successfully processed, causing it to be skipped permanently once committed. This is verifiable in the new `queue_consumer.py` except block in `submit`. The same pattern exists in `OrderedQueueWorker.run` where `complete_offset` is called in `finally` even when `result_processor` raises, contradicting the class docstring promise "Only commits offsets after successful processing."

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets breaks at the first offset in [start, max_offset] that was never added via add_offset, and nothing ever fills that gap, so commits stall permanently at any missing offset. Real Kafka topics produce offset gaps (aborted transactions, log compaction); the new test_offset_gaps tests bake gap-blocking in as expected behavior, but unlike arroyo's built-in modes (which commit past gaps), this consumer's commits stop forever at the gap, causing unbounded consumer lag and unbounded growth of all_offsets until manual intervention — the tests' assumption that submitted offsets are gap-free-by-design does not hold for the production topic.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets iterates from `start` to `max_offset` and `break`s if an offset is either outstanding OR not present in `all_offsets` (`if offset in all_offsets and offset not in outstanding: ... else: break`). That means if the consumer ever observes offsets like {100, 102, 103} (i.e., a missing 101 that is never added via add_offset), commits will never advance past 100 because the loop stops at the first missing offset. The new tests explicitly encode this “gap blocks commits” behavior (e.g., `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` and uptime `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps`), so it appears intentional in this PR rather than an accidental defect. However, it is a real, diff-grounded concern/assumption: the strategy cannot progress commits past permanently missing offsets unless they later arrive, which could be problematic depending on real offset-delivery semantics.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() with no maxsize while SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' — no backpressure exists. When workers fall behind (e.g., a slow downstream in result_processor or a single hot subscription hashing to one queue), the affected queue grows without bound, consuming unbounded memory in the consumer process and eventually OOM-killing it, with no lag-based protection the docstring promises.

adjudication.rationale: In `FixedQueuePool.__init__`, each worker queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, so it is unbounded. `FixedQueuePool.submit` always does `work_queue.put(work_item)` (blocking only if bounded/full, which never happens here), so there is no queue-level backpressure. This directly contradicts `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`'s docstring claim of “Natural backpressure when queues fill up” and can allow unbounded in-memory growth if producers outpace `OrderedQueueWorker` processing (e.g., a hot group_key mapped to one queue).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] submit passes message.payload directly to the decoder, but the production decoder (ResultsStrategyFactory.decode_payload) asserts not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload), so every FilteredPayload message raises AssertionError and is routed into the exception path. Every filtered message in production is logged as 'Error submitting message to queue' with a full stack trace (error-log spam proportional to filtered volume) and handled as a failure instead of the no-op the strategy's unit-test decoder implements; the unit test test_handles_invalid_messages only passes because it substitutes a custom decoder that does not have this assertion.

adjudication.rationale: In `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit`, the strategy calls `result = self.decoder(message.payload)` with `message.payload` typed as `KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload`. In production wiring (`ResultsStrategyFactory.create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`), `decoder` is `partial(self.decode_payload, self.topic_for_codec)`, and `decode_payload` contains `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)`. Therefore, any `FilteredPayload` message will raise `AssertionError`, be caught by the broad `except Exception:` in `submit`, and trigger `logger.exception("Error submitting message to queue")` (stack trace) rather than the intended `result is None` no-op path. The unit test `test_handles_invalid_messages` passes only because it supplies a custom decoder that explicitly returns `None` for `FilteredPayload`, masking this production behavior mismatch.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] self.result_processor = self.result_processor_cls() was moved from the end of __init__ to the top, before max_batch_size/max_batch_time/input_block_size/output_block_size are assigned, to satisfy the new queue_pool branch. Any result_processor_cls whose constructor reads those attributes now observes pre-assignment values (None/defaults) in every mode, not just thread-queue-parallel — a silent initialization-order change to all existing serial/parallel/batched-parallel consumers introduced as a side effect of the new mode, who get bitten when a subclass constructor depends on that config.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows an initialization-order change in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`: `self.result_processor = self.result_processor_cls()` is now executed immediately after `self.mode` (and before `max_batch_size/max_batch_time/max_workers/input_block_size/output_block_size` are applied). Previously it was at the end of `__init__`. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral change that could affect any `result_processor_cls.__init__` that reads factory attributes set later, but the diff does not show any such constructor, so an actual breakage cannot be verified from the PR alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool shutdown ownership is split between ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown (which also nulls the reference) and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close/join, both of which shut down the same shared pool instance. In the normal arroyo lifecycle close() then join() (which calls close() again) shut the pool down twice per run, and factory.shutdown() plus strategy.close() in the tests exercise a third path; worse, if arroyo invokes create_with_partitions again after a close (restart within the process), the new strategy receives the already-shut-down pool whose workers have exited, so messages queue but are never processed and offsets never commit.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ResultsStrategyFactory` creates and stores a single shared `FixedQueuePool` instance on `self.queue_pool` in `__init__` when `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"`, and `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` passes that same instance into each new `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy`. But `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` and does not clear/recreate it. Therefore, if the factory is reused to call `create_with_partitions` again after a previous strategy was closed, the new strategy will receive an already-shutdown pool (workers stopped), so submitted work items may enqueue without being processed and offsets may never advance. Additionally, `join()` calls `close()`, so an arroyo lifecycle that calls `close()` then `join()` would shut the same pool down twice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts that no commit occurs after a processing failure, which is the opposite of the implementation's behavior (the failed offset is completed and becomes committable). The test encodes drifted intent ('errors block commits') that the code does not implement; it only passes when the loop breaks before the commit thread's next 1-second tick, making it timing-flaky, and it documents a guarantee ('Only commits offsets after successful processing') that the shipped code violates — whoever trusts the test or the docstring will be wrong.
matched_golden_ids: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The golden issue is that the test’s docstring does not align with what the test/code actually do. The candidate explicitly states the docstring claims “Only commits offsets after successful processing” but the implementation allows committing after a failure, indicating the documented intent is drifted/mismatched. That is the same underlying mismatch concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty is never called anywhere in the diff (production code or tests). Dead code that implies a drain-before-shutdown behavior that shutdown() does not actually provide (shutdown discards queued items without waiting); deleting the method removes a misleading surface — the next reader may assume graceful drain exists when it does not.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty` (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py) but there are no call sites in the production changes or the new tests; the tests poll `get_stats()` directly and then call `shutdown()`. This makes `wait_until_empty` dead code in this PR. Also, `shutdown()` sets each worker’s `shutdown` flag and shuts down the queues, so it does not clearly guarantee draining queued items before stopping workers, making the presence of `wait_until_empty` potentially misleading about available “drain-before-shutdown” behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] WorkItem.message is populated on every submit but never read by any code in the diff. Every queued item retains the full Kafka Message (payload bytes included) in memory for the entire queue dwell time; deleting the field shrinks per-item memory and removes dead state — this compounds the unbounded-queue memory growth since payloads are held twice (payload and result).

adjudication.rationale: In `queue_consumer.py`, `WorkItem` includes a `message: Message[KafkaPayload | FilteredPayload]` field, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` always populates it when creating `WorkItem(...)`. However, the worker (`OrderedQueueWorker.run`) only uses `work_item.result` plus `work_item.partition/offset` for offset tracking; no code in the diff reads `work_item.message`. Since the queues are created as unbounded `queue.Queue()` instances, retaining the full Kafka `Message` (including payload bytes) per queued item can unnecessarily increase memory usage during queue dwell time; removing the unused field would reduce per-item memory.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The generic OrderedQueueWorker hardcodes a 'monitors.' prefix into the sentry_sdk transaction name (f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}") for a component used by non-monitors consumers such as the uptime results consumer. Uptime (and any future ResultsStrategyFactory consumer) trace transactions are mislabeled under the monitors namespace, so engineers filtering dashboards/alerts by transaction name for the uptime consumer will not find or will misattribute its worker spans.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `OrderedQueueWorker.run` (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py), the Sentry transaction name is hardcoded as `name=f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`. This queue worker is used by `ResultsStrategyFactory` when `mode == "thread-queue-parallel"` (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py), including the uptime results consumer (tests show `identifier` like "uptime"). That means uptime processing will emit transactions under the `monitors.*` namespace (e.g., `monitors.uptime.worker_0`), which is a concrete, diff-grounded observability/labeling issue but not a functional correctness defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OrderedQueueWorker.run emits the remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth gauge inside the finally block, i.e., once per processed item per worker thread. Metric emission volume scales linearly with message throughput across all queue workers instead of being sampled or emitted from poll(), adding measurable metrics cost and cardinality on the hottest path in the consumer.

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py`, `OrderedQueueWorker.run` unconditionally calls `metrics.gauge("remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth", self.work_queue.qsize(), tags={...})` in the `finally` block for every dequeued `WorkItem` (i.e., per message processed per worker thread). This places metric emission on the hottest per-item path and scales directly with throughput across all workers, rather than being emitted at a lower cadence (e.g., from `poll()` like `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.poll` does for `remote_subscriptions.queue_pool.total_queued`). This is a concrete performance/observability-cost concern introduced by the diff, not a functional correctness bug.
